extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of early-18th-century social essays, dramatists and poets, and literate coffee-house society
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical principles for composing tragedy and related literary pieces—emphasizing authentic emotional expression, appropriate authorial sympathy, and models (Shakespeare). Also includes related social-writing maxims (portrayal of love vs lust; handling fops; moral alignment of conscience/honour/credit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression over description in tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is the common fault...that you give us rather the sentiments of such who behold tragical events, than of such who bear a part in them themselves."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers of tragedy should present the direct, inward expression of sorrow from those who experience it, not the detached impressions of observers. "You must go to the very bottom of the heart, or it is all mere language;" avoid simulated grief—"he who pretends to be sorrowful, and is not, is a wretch yet more contemptible than he who pretends to be merry, and is not." Read Shakespeare for models (example: Morton's scene in 2 Henry IV) and aim for the authentic eruption of feeling rather than ornamental description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writer must discover and reveal meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: "to write without discovering your meaning, bears a just resemblance to marching without beat of drum."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A piece of writing should have a clear discovered purpose or meaning; aim for intentionality and clarity in composition. (Related note: prefer a postscript apology to preemptive excuses—don't excuse before the offence is committed.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial sympathy appropriate to the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: "He who describes the concern of great men, must have a soul as noble, and as susceptible of high thoughts, as they whom he represents."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To represent heroic or elevated subjects convincingly, the writer must possess or summon comparable depth and nobility of feeling and thought; lacking that capacity, choose less exalted subjects. (Author's consequence: lay aside his high tragedy until he can match the 'soul' of his heroes.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Read Shakespeare with care as corrective model
rubrics_metrics.description: "I would advise all who pretend this way, to read Shakespeare with care, and they will soon be deterred from putting forth what is usually called 'tragedy.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Shakespeare as a schooling in authentic tragic presentation and restraint; study his scenes (e.g. Morton's restraint and subsequent abandonment in 2 Henry IV) to learn how to convey genuine passion rather than rhetorical description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as remedy for spleen (use art to affect emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The spleen is not to be cured by medicine, but by poetry."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author advances that poetry (and music) can remedy melancholy more effectively than physical medicines; when treating poetical vapours or melancholy in writing or life, use poetic means. A practical aphorism: choose a 'physician' who has experienced the malady himself—i.e., an artist who understands the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish love from lust in depiction and moral judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: "Love is a beauteous blind child... Lust... in the form of a satyr... part human, part bestial."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying interpersonal passion, treat 'love' as innocent, ennobling, and stabilizing (produces decency and mutual good), whereas 'lust' is bestial, exploitative, jealous, and destructive. Use character examples (Aspasia as ideal love; Corinna, Limberham, Messalina as examples of lust/kept-woman pathology) to show consequences and moral distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct social handling of fops and coxcombs
rubrics_metrics.description: "It will be much more easy therefore to laugh him into reason, than convert him from his foppery by any serious contempt."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dealing with vanity and affectation (fops), use ridicule and lightness rather than heavy contempt—public mockery that is mild can reform; serious disdain often entrenches the folly. (Anecdote: Sir Taffety Trippet and the Tunbridge lovers.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience, honour, and credit must align; act by reason not opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: "The world will never be in any manner of order or tranquillity, till men are firmly convinced, that conscience, honour, and credit, are all in one interest; and that without the concurrence of the former, the latter are but impositions upon ourselves and others."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate characters and social practices by whether conscience governs behaviour, not mere appearance or public opinion. The allegory of Alethes (Conscience), Verisimilis (appearance/honour), and Umbra (credit) shows the perils when honour/credit become instruments of ambition rather than reflections of conscience. Encourage acting from reason and reflection rather than seeking approval or reputation alone.
